title: Ice Excavation
strapline: Treasure frozen deep in a block of ice — and every tool and trick you can find to free it.
intent: Freeing objects frozen inside ice is an irresistible, purposeful challenge that keeps children persisting long after other activities would end.
Discovering what melts the ice fastest — warm water, salt, hands, hammering, breath — is genuine scientific testing of cause and effect.
Chipping, pouring and rubbing to free the treasure builds hand strength, tool control and determined fine-motor work.
The dramatic change from solid to liquid, and the cold on their hands, gives children vivid first-hand experience of states of matter and temperature.
It is a rich source of describing language — frozen, melting, slippery, cracking, dripping — anchored in something happening right now.
Working out and comparing melting strategies invites prediction, cooperation and celebrating the eventual rescue together.
implementation: Freeze small-world animals, gems or letters into blocks or balloons of ice the night before, and present them as treasure to be freed.
Offer a range of tools and 'melters' — warm water in droppers, salt, small hammers, spoons, brushes — and let children test which works.
Ask them to predict and compare: 'which do you think will free it fastest — the warm water or the salt?'
Narrate the change: 'it's melting — feel the water, it was solid ice a minute ago'.
Let children work at it as long as they want; the persistence is a huge part of the value.
Talk about cold, freezing and melting in the wider world — puddles in winter, the freezer, an ice lolly.
key_questions: Which do you think will free it fastest — the warm water or the salt?
It was solid ice a minute ago — feel it now, what's happening?
What could we use to melt it more quickly?
Which melted first, and which is taking the longest?
How did you finally free your treasure?

impact.text: Children test what melts ice fastest — warm water, salt, hands, hammering — genuine cause and effect.
Children chip, pour and rub to free the treasure, building hand strength and determined fine-motor work.
Children experience the change from solid to liquid first-hand, feeling cold and temperature.
Children predict and compare melting strategies, cooperating and celebrating the rescue.
Children gain describing words — frozen, melting, slippery, cracking, dripping.

enhancements: Small-world animals, gems or letters frozen into ice blocks or balloons the night before.
A range of 'melters' — warm water in droppers, salt, small hammers, spoons, brushes.
A prediction chart for which method children think will win.
A link to cold in the wider world — winter puddles, the freezer, an ice lolly.
Coloured ice so the melting is easier to watch.

playing_exploring: Children throw everything they have at the ice — tools, warm water, salt, sheer effort — to see what works.
The frozen treasure is an irresistible, hands-on puzzle.
active_learning: Freeing the treasure takes real persistence, and children stay with it, celebrating hard-won progress.
creating_thinking: Children predict which method will melt the ice fastest, test their ideas and compare what actually happens.
